pages.text: The school radio club had a new programme to make: “Voices Along the River”. Kyei held the recorder. Naa Shika held the notebook. “Rule one,” she said. “We check every fact and we say where it came from.” Kyei pressed record. “Rule two,” he said. “We are kind, even when we disagree.” Their first interview was with a real reporter.

pages.text: Aunty Gloria, a radio journalist, shook their hands. “A good report has three parts,” she said. “What happened. Who says so. And how we know. If we do not know, we say that. I report on galamsey, and I stay safe by working in a team, telling my editor where I am, and never going to a site alone. Protecting sources is also part of my job.” Naa Shika wrote it all down.

pages.text: Next, they met Dr Nketia, an invented scientist from a university. “Science is like a river,” he said. “It flows slowly and carries many findings. One research team found heavy metals in placentas from mothers in galamsey areas. Paediatricians warn that children may be affected in other ways, but they also say we need more studies. It is important not to say more than the evidence says.”

pages.text: Kyei’s aunt was a member of a church that had joined an Environmental Prayer Walk in Accra on 11 October 2024. “Thousands of people walked quietly, and the bishops presented a petition,” she said. “They asked for stronger protection of water bodies and an end to galamsey. A priest said that the fight belongs to everyone. It was peaceful, and many groups joined.”

pages.text: Naa Shika’s cousin had joined a protest in September 2024. “It did not go smoothly,” she said. “A court order stopped the planned protest site. On one day, some protesters blocked roads, and the police made arrests. Reports say about fifty-four people were arrested, thirty-nine were taken to court and remanded for twelve days. Lawyers said some had no access to food or family, and the police denied that. People gave different accounts.”

pages.alt: A group of young people hold banners on a road while a police line stands at a distance, drawn calmly and without violence.

pages.text: “Why are you telling us both?” asked Kyei. “Because it is true that people disagree,” said Naa Shika’s cousin. “Peaceful protest is a right, and so is the duty to obey the law. Media rights groups said everyone’s rights must be respected, and they asked for an independent inquiry into what happened. A good citizen can hold both ideas: protest peacefully, and ask for fair treatment.”

pages.text: Back in the radio room, Naa Shika sorted her notes into three columns: Facts, Claims and Opinions. “Heavy metals found in placentas” went under Facts. “Some say officials are involved” went under Claims. “Galamsey must end now” went under Opinions. “We say which is which,” she told Kyei. “Otherwise, listeners might think that every sentence has the same weight.”

pages.text: The programme aired on Friday. It ended with a message from Kyei: “Your voice matters. Ask questions. Check facts. Protect the river. And be kind to those who disagree with you.” The next morning, the headteacher announced that the club would visit a district assembly meeting. Naa Shika grinned. “Next, we ask the leaders,” she said. The end.
